🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

John Locke lived in England more than three hundred years ago, in a time of civil war, when kings and parliaments fought over who should rule. He asked a simple question: why should anyone obey a government at all?

Locke imagined people long ago with no kings and no laws written down. He called this the state of nature. Even then, he said, people knew a rule written by reason: don't hurt other people in their life, health, freedom or belongings.

But in the state of nature there is no judge. If someone takes your apples, you must settle it yourself, and that leads to fights. So people agree together to set up a government to make fair laws and judge fairly. Locke said a government gets its power from that agreement, which he called consent.

blocks.name: gb-locke-path
blocks.cap: Step through Locke's story of how government begins, and what happens if it breaks its trust.

blocks.html: Locke also wrote a letter about religion. He said that you can't force someone to truly believe something. A ruler can make people say words or go to a building, but belief happens inside the mind.

🧩 Try this

The apple-tree game. Pick an apple (or a pinecone) that nobody owns. Locke said it becomes yours when you mix your work with it, by picking it. But he added a rule: you must leave enough and as good for others, and not take more than you can use before it spoils. Talk together: what would be fair if there were only three apples and five people?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: A book written in a dangerous time

blocks.html: Locke (1632–1704) wrote the Two Treatises of Government during the struggles between King Charles II, his brother James II and Parliament. He published them without his name in 1689, after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 replaced James with William and Mary. The First Treatise answers Sir Robert Filmer, who had argued that kings inherit their power from Adam. The Second Treatise, the one most read today, gives Locke's own account. The same year he published A Letter Concerning Toleration, first in Latin, then in William Popple's English translation.

blocks.text: The state of nature and its law

blocks.html: Locke begins with people as they would be without any government: free and equal, with no one naturally set over anyone else. That is a state of liberty, he says, but not of license, because a law of nature binds everyone even there:

For Locke this law rests on God: people are the "workmanship" of one Maker, so no one may treat another as made for his own use. He also argues that in the state of nature each person may punish those who break the law of nature. The trouble is that people judge their own cases, and they are partial to themselves.
Locke's chapter on property explains how something the earth gives to everyone in common can become one person's own. His answer is labor:

He adds limits: there must be "enough, and as good" left for others, and no one may take more than he can use before it spoils. Money, he argues, changed things, because gold and silver don't spoil, so people could gather more than they could use.

Locke's key terms. State of nature: life without a common judge. Law of nature: the moral law reason teaches. Property: in Locke's wide sense, a person's "life, liberty and estate." Consent: agreeing to join a political society. Trust: the government holds its power in trust for the people's good.

People join together and set up a legislature, the supreme power, to make settled, known laws, with impartial judges and the force to carry out the law. The legislature may not rule by sudden decrees, take people's property without their consent (for example, taxes need the consent of the people or their representatives), or hand its law-making power to others. Locke also separates the executive power (carrying out the laws) from the legislative.

And if a government breaks its trust, aiming at the lives, liberties or goods of the people, then, Locke argues, it dissolves itself, and the people may set up a new one. He insists this is not for small mistakes, but for "a long train of abuses."

blocks.name: gb-locke-path
blocks.cap: The whole argument as a path: state of nature, its troubles, consent, government in trust, and the right of a people when the trust is broken.

blocks.html: Locke argues that the government's job is to protect "civil interests": life, liberty, health and possessions. The care of souls belongs to each person and to churches, which are voluntary societies. His main reason is about the mind itself:

Locke's toleration had limits that later readers have noted. He would not tolerate those who denied God, since he thought their promises could not be trusted, nor churches he believed owed obedience to a foreign ruler, which in his England meant chiefly Roman Catholics. Later thinkers widened the idea of religious freedom well beyond his.

Thinking Locke said people may overthrow any government they dislike. He says the right comes only when a government acts against the very purpose for which it was trusted, after a long train of abuses, and he expected people to be slow to use it.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Readers have long heard Locke in the American Declaration of Independence (1776): people equal by nature, rights to life and liberty, government by consent, and a right to alter or abolish a government that destroys those ends. Historians debate how much the founders drew on Locke directly and how much on other sources, such as English common law, classical republican writers and their own colonial charters. The American State Papers rung, later in this era, takes up the documents themselves.

Some critics say the state of nature never existed as a real time in history; Locke answered that independent rulers are in a state of nature with each other even now. David Hume, later on this ladder, doubted that most governments began by consent at all and said they rest mostly on habit and the benefits they bring. Others question the labor theory of property: does mixing labor with something make it yours, or do you just lose your labor? Locke's defenders reply that his account explains why taking someone's work without consent seems wrong.

Readers also notice a tension: Locke wrote about natural freedom, yet he helped draft the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina (1669) and invested in a company that traded in enslaved people. Historians discuss how he reconciled these, and many conclude that he did not.

items: Can people consent to a government just by living under it? Locke called this "tacit consent." Is that enough?
When, if ever, may people resist their government?
Why might forcing belief fail even on its own terms?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What would be hard about living with no judges and no laws written down?
  2. Locke says picking an apple makes it yours. Do you agree? What if it grew in someone's yard?
  3. Why do you think Locke said you can't force someone to truly believe something?
  4. What does it mean for a government to hold power "in trust"?
  5. Is there a difference between obeying a rule because you agreed to it and obeying because you are afraid?
  6. Locke didn't extend toleration to everyone. Why do you think ideas like this often grow wider over time?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Where do your ideas come from? Were you born knowing what red is, or what a lemon tastes like? John Locke said no. He said a baby's mind is like a sheet of blank white paper, and experience writes on it.
Experience comes in two ways. Sensation is what your senses bring in: colors, sounds, tastes, hot and cold. Reflection is noticing what your own mind does: thinking, remembering, wanting, doubting.
Locke said simple ideas are like building blocks. Your mind puts them together to make bigger ideas. "Apple" is red + round + sweet + crunchy + a certain smell, all joined together.

blocks.name: gb-idea-builder
blocks.cap: Pick simple ideas and watch the mind join them into a complex idea.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Mystery bag. Put a few things in a bag (a spoon, an orange, a feather). Without looking, one person feels an object and names only simple ideas: "cold, smooth, hard, curved." Can the others guess it? Then talk: could you know what an orange is if you had never seen, smelled, touched or tasted one?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: A book that began with a puzzle

blocks.html: Locke tells us the Essay (1689) began when friends meeting in his room got stuck on a hard question. He suggested they should first find out what the human mind is fit to know. Nearly twenty years later the answer filled four books.

Many thinkers held that some ideas and principles are stamped on the mind at birth, such as "whatever is, is" or the idea of God. Locke argues against this. If such ideas were innate, children and every people on earth would know them, and they plainly don't. Better, he says, to see how the mind gets its ideas.

blocks.text: Book II: all ideas from experience

blocks.html: The two "fountains" are sensation and reflection. From them come simple ideas, which the mind can't make up itself, and from those the mind builds complex ideas by combining, comparing and abstracting: ideas of substances (gold, a horse), of modes (a dozen, beauty, a lie) and of relations (father, bigger, cause).

blocks.name: gb-idea-builder
blocks.cap: Choose a thing, then switch its simple ideas on and off. Which ones come from sensation, and which from reflection?

blocks.html: Locke draws a famous line. Primary qualities, such as solidity, size, shape, motion and number, are really in objects, and our ideas of them resemble them. Secondary qualities, such as colors, sounds, tastes, smells and warmth, are powers in objects to produce ideas in us. There is no "sweetness" in sugar the way there is shape in it. Locke uses a simple test: the same water can feel warm to one hand and cold to the other.

head: Primary (in the thing)
Secondary (powers to cause ideas in us)
blocks.cap: Locke's two kinds of qualities

blocks.text: Persons, words and the limits of knowledge

blocks.html: In a famous chapter Locke asks what makes you the same person over time. Not the same body or even the same soul-stuff, he says, but the same consciousness: what you can remember as your own. Book III warns that many quarrels come from words used without clear ideas. Book IV says knowledge is the perception that ideas agree or disagree, and that it is narrower than we hope. Where we lack knowledge, we must live by probability and judgment, holding beliefs with the strength the evidence gives.
Thinking Locke said the mind is passive. The "white paper" receives simple ideas, but the mind is busy: it compares, combines, abstracts and reflects on its own operations.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Essay made Locke the leader of what later historians call British empiricism, the view that knowledge comes from experience. George Berkeley and David Hume, the next two rungs, start from Locke and push his ideas further. Berkeley asked why primary qualities should be any different from secondary ones. Hume asked where our idea of cause comes from. Kant, later in this era, tried to show that experience alone can't explain how we know some things for certain.

Locke's account of personal identity is still discussed by philosophers, as are his ideas on education (in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, 1693), which shaped how many families taught their children.

Leibniz wrote a long reply, New Essays on Human Understanding, arguing that the mind is more like a block of marble with veins in it: it has tendencies that experience brings out. Modern research on infants finds that babies come ready to learn some things quickly, such as faces and language sounds, which many take as a partial answer to Locke, though the debate about what is inborn continues.

items: Is there anything you know that didn't come from experience?
If you lost all your memories, would you still be the same person?
Is the redness of an apple in the apple, or in you?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is the earliest thing you remember learning? How did you learn it?
  2. Can you imagine a color you have never seen? Why or why not?
  3. Locke said many arguments come from people using words differently. Can you think of an example?
  4. Is a strawberry's sweetness in the strawberry or in you? What would Locke say?
  5. What makes you the same person you were when you were five?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

George Berkeley was an Irish bishop with a surprising idea. Think about a table. You can see it, touch it, knock on it. But what is the table, apart from what you see and feel and hear? Berkeley said: nothing. For things like tables, to be is to be perceived.

That sounds strange! Does the table vanish when everyone leaves the room? Berkeley said no, because God always perceives everything. So the world is real and steady, but it is made of ideas in minds, not of some hidden "matter" behind them.

Berkeley liked a test with water. Make one hand warm and the other cold, then put both in the same bowl of lukewarm water. One hand says "cold!" and the other says "warm!" Which is right? Berkeley said heat and cold are in our feelings, not out in the water.

blocks.name: gb-water-hands
blocks.cap: Warm one hand and cool the other, then dip both in the same water. What does each hand feel?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The three-bowl test. With a grown-up, set out three bowls: cool water, lukewarm water and warm (not hot) tap water. Hold one hand in the cool bowl and one in the warm bowl for a minute, then put both into the lukewarm bowl. What does each hand tell you?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Berkeley (1685–1753) was 25 and a fellow of Trinity College, Dublin, when he published the Principles of Human Knowledge in 1710. He later became Bishop of Cloyne, spent three years in Rhode Island planning a college in Bermuda that never opened, and gave his library and farm to Yale. He wrote the Principles to answer skeptics and those who doubted God, and he expected his idea to bring philosophy back to common sense.

blocks.text: To be is to be perceived

blocks.html: Berkeley starts from Locke: what we know directly are ideas. Then he asks what it means to say a sensible thing exists:
Esse est percipi is Latin for "to be is to be perceived." Berkeley says this of sensible things. Minds, which he calls spirits, are different: their being is to perceive and to act.

Locke had said colors and tastes are only in us but shape and size are really in things. Berkeley replies that we can't even imagine a shape with no color, or a size apart from how it looks or feels. And shapes and sizes change with where we stand, just as colors change with the light. So if secondary qualities are only in the mind, primary ones are too. "Matter" as something unthinking, unseen and unfelt behind our ideas is, he says, an empty word.

blocks.name: gb-water-hands
blocks.cap: Berkeley's argument from the bowl of water: the same water can't be both warm and cold, so warmth must be in the feeling.

blocks.html: If tables are ideas, why can't I wish them away? Because, Berkeley answers, ideas of sense are not made by my will. They come in a steady, lawful order from another mind, God. What scientists call the laws of nature are the regular ways God gives us ideas. Science still works; it studies these regularities. What goes away, Berkeley says, is an unseen matter that explains nothing.

Thinking Berkeley said the world is a dream or that nothing is real. He said the opposite: the things we see and touch are real, and are exactly what they seem. What he denied was matter existing apart from all minds.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Samuel Johnson, the subject of the Boswell rung, is said to have kicked a large stone and said, "I refute it thus." Berkeley's defenders say this misses the point: Berkeley never denied that stones feel solid. David Hume, the next rung, praised Berkeley's arguments but turned them in a skeptical direction, and Kant later tried to separate his own view from Berkeley's.

Berkeley is often called the founder of idealism, the view that reality is fundamentally mental. Most philosophers today don't accept his conclusion, but his questions about perception, what we can know of things apart from experience, are still argued over. His Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713) present the same ideas in a livelier form and appear in the Harvard Classics readings.

items: How could you prove that your room is still there when no one is in it?
Is a color in an object, or in the eye, or in the mind?
Does science need the idea of matter, or only the regular order of what we observe?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. If a tree falls in a forest and no one hears it, does it make a sound? What would Berkeley say?
  2. In the water test, which hand is telling the truth?
  3. Can you picture a shape with no color at all?
  4. Why did Berkeley think his view helped people trust that God exists?
  5. Johnson kicked a stone to answer Berkeley. Was that a good answer?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
When one billiard ball hits another, the second one rolls away. You knew that would happen. But how did you know? David Hume, a Scottish thinker, asked this question and gave a surprising answer.

Hume said we never actually see one ball make the other move. We see ball one move, we see the touch, and we see ball two move. That's all. After seeing this many times, our mind gets used to it and expects it. Hume called this habit custom.
So we learn about the world only by experience, and custom is "the great guide of human life." It works very well. But Hume said it is a habit, not a proof.

blocks.name: gb-billiards
blocks.cap: Strike the ball and watch. Each time, count what you actually see. Do you ever see the push itself?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Guess what happens. Show a child something they have never seen: a magnet near a paper clip, or baking soda dropped in vinegar (with a grown-up). Before doing it, ask them to guess what will happen. Could they know without ever having seen it? Then do it twice more. Notice how quickly we start to expect it.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: A philosopher who wanted to be read

blocks.html: Hume (1711–1776) first put his ideas in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), which, he said, "fell dead-born from the press." He rewrote the first part more briefly and clearly as An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748). He also wrote a bestselling History of England and essays on politics and economics, and was a close friend of Adam Smith.

Hume divides what is in the mind into impressions, our lively perceptions when we see, hear, feel or want, and ideas, their fainter copies in memory and thought. Every simple idea comes from an impression. So to test a puzzling idea, ask: from what impression is it copied? If none, the word may have no meaning.

All reasoning, Hume says, is about one of two things. Relations of ideas, such as "three times five is half of thirty," are known by thought alone; denying them is a contradiction. Matters of fact, such as "the sun will rise tomorrow," are known only by experience; their opposite is always conceivable.

head: Relations of ideas
Matters of fact
rows: the sun will rise; fire burns; bread nourishes
blocks.cap: Hume's fork

blocks.html: All our reasoning about matters of fact rests on cause and effect. But where does that idea come from? Not from reason alone:

Nor from a single experience, since we see only one event following another, never a hidden power or "necessary connexion" between them. Even after many experiences, reasoning can't prove that the future will resemble the past, because any argument for that would already assume it. What carries us from past to future is custom:

blocks.name: gb-billiards
blocks.cap: The idea of cause, in Hume's terms: contact, one event after another, and a constant conjunction we have seen many times. Count the trials, and notice what you never see.

blocks.html: In Section X Hume argues that testimony for a miracle, a violation of a law of nature, must be weighed against all the uniform experience that established that law; a wise person proportions belief to the evidence. Religious readers have answered this argument from his day to ours, and it remains one of the most debated pages he wrote.

Hume did not want people to stop believing in the world. Nature, he said, is too strong for that. He recommends a mitigated skepticism: modest, careful, and limited to subjects our minds can handle. He ends with a famous, sharp test for books:

Thinking Hume said causes don't exist. He said we can't prove by reason that causes must work the same way tomorrow, and that our idea of cause comes from constant conjunction and custom. He relied on causal reasoning in everything he did.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Philosophers call Hume's puzzle about the future "the problem of induction." Kant said Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber" and wrote the Critique of Pure Reason partly in answer. In the 20th century some philosophers argued that science advances by testing and trying to refute guesses rather than proving them, while others defend probability-based accounts of how evidence supports theories. No answer has satisfied everyone.

Thomas Reid, another Scot, argued that Hume's starting point, that we know only our own impressions and ideas, leads to absurd results, and that common sense beliefs deserve trust. Defenders of miracles, from George Campbell in Hume's day onward, argued that his test sets the bar so that no testimony could ever be enough. Hume's admirers answer that he asks only for evidence in proportion to the claim.

items: How do you know the sun will rise tomorrow?
Is believing something out of habit the same as believing it without reason?
What kind of evidence would it take to believe something very surprising?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What have you learned only by seeing it happen many times?
  2. Can you imagine water running uphill? Does imagining it make it possible?
  3. Why might a habit of expecting things be useful even if it isn't a proof?
  4. Hume said a wise person proportions belief to the evidence. What does that mean in everyday life?
  5. Was Hume right to say some books should be "committed to the flames"? What do you think he meant?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Immanuel Kant lived his whole life in one city, Königsberg, in Prussia. People said he walked at the same time every day so exactly that neighbors set their clocks by him. But in his head he made a huge journey.

Kant noticed something about how we know things. Imagine you always wore blue glasses that you could never take off. Everything you saw would look blue. You could be sure, before you looked, that the next thing you saw would look blue, because the blue comes from the glasses.

Kant said our minds work a bit like that. Everything we experience comes to us arranged in space and time, and connected by cause and effect. That's why we can be sure of some things before we look, like that 7 + 5 will always make 12, or that every event has a cause.

blocks.name: gb-kant-lenses
blocks.cap: Turn the mind's "lenses" on and off and see what experience would be like without them.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Colored glasses. Look through a piece of colored cellophane or a colored bottle. Before you look at the next thing, predict its color. How did you know? Then talk about it: Kant said space and time are like glasses we can never take off. Can you imagine something that is in no place and at no time?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Kant (1724–1804) taught at the university in Königsberg for decades. At 57 he published the Critique of Pure Reason (1781; much-revised second edition 1787). It is one of the hardest books on this ladder, and one of the most influential. Kant said reading Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber": if all knowledge came from experience, how could we know anything to be necessary and universal?

Kant sorts judgments two ways. A priori means known independently of experience; a posteriori, known from experience. Analytic means the predicate is already contained in the subject ("all bodies are extended"); synthetic means it adds something new ("all bodies are heavy"). The big question of the book is: how are synthetic a priori judgments possible? Kant thinks mathematics ("7 + 5 = 12", "a straight line is the shortest between two points") and the first principles of physics ("every event has a cause") are exactly such judgments.

head: Analytic
Synthetic
rows: this rose is red; bodies are heavy
blocks.cap: Kant's table of judgments, with examples

blocks.html: Like Copernicus, who explained the heavens by moving the observer, Kant explains necessary knowledge by looking at the knower. Space and time are the mind's forms of intuition, the way anything must appear to us. The categories, such as unity, substance and cause, are the mind's concepts for joining appearances into one experience. Both are needed:

blocks.name: gb-kant-lenses
blocks.cap: Sensation supplies the matter; space and time give it form; the categories join it into objects connected by cause. Switch a layer off to see what goes missing.

blocks.html: The price of this answer is a limit. We know things only as they appear to us, never as things in themselves. When reason tries to go beyond any possible experience, to prove that the soul is immortal, that the world had a beginning, or that God exists, it falls into illusions and contradictions, which Kant sets out as the antinomies: equally strong proofs on both sides, for instance that the world had a beginning in time and that it did not. In Meiklejohn's translation, Kant says he must "abolish knowledge, to make room for belief": these questions can't be settled by theoretical proof either way, and he took them up again in his moral philosophy.

Thinking Kant said the world is made up by each person's imagination. He held that the forms of space, time and the categories are the same for every human knower, which is why science is objective and shared.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Critique started a long debate. German idealists such as Fichte and Hegel (in the next era) dropped the thing in itself and built vast systems on the mind's activity. Others objected that Kant's list of twelve categories looks arbitrary. When mathematicians later developed non-Euclidean geometries and Einstein used one in physics, many concluded that Kant was wrong that Euclid's geometry is known a priori of space, while Kant's defenders reply that his deeper point about the mind's part in experience survives.
Kant's distinction between the questions science can answer and those it can't still shapes how many people think about science and religion.

items: Can we know anything for certain before we experience it?
If we know only how things appear to us, does it matter what they are in themselves?
Why might reason contradict itself when it asks whether the universe had a beginning?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. How do you know that 7 + 5 = 12 will be true tomorrow?
  2. Can you imagine something that isn't anywhere and isn't at any time?
  3. Kant compared his idea to Copernicus moving the Earth. What did he "move"?
  4. Why do you think Kant set limits on what reason can know?
  5. Thoughts without content are empty, Kant says. What do you think that means?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Suppose you could tell a lie and get something you want, and no one would ever find out. Would it be all right? Immanuel Kant said there is a test you can use.

Ask: What if everybody did this? If everyone told lies whenever it helped them, no one would believe anybody, and lying wouldn't even work anymore. So, Kant said, the rule "lie when it helps me" fails the test.
Kant had a second way to say the same thing: treat people as people, never just as tools for getting what you want. A friend is not a ladder to climb.

blocks.name: gb-maxim-test
blocks.cap: Choose a rule for acting and run Kant's test: could everyone follow it?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The everybody test. Write some rules on cards: "Cut in line when I'm in a hurry," "Say thank you when someone helps me," "Borrow things and never give them back," "Help someone who drops their books." Take turns drawing a card and imagining a world where everyone follows it. Which worlds work? Which ones fall apart?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Volume 39 gathers Kant's ethics: the Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals (1785; also called the Groundwork), the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), and parts of The Metaphysics of Morals (1797) on law, rights and virtue. Kant wanted to find the supreme principle of morality, one that holds for every rational being, not just for people who happen to want certain things.

A good will is good not because of what it achieves but because of how it wills: it acts from duty, out of respect for the moral law. Kant's example: a shopkeeper who gives children correct change only because it's good for business does the right thing, but his action has no special moral worth. One who would be honest even when it costs him acts from duty.
Many commands are hypothetical: "If you want to be healthy, exercise." They bind only if you want the goal. Morality, Kant says, commands categorically, with no "if":

A maxim is the personal rule behind an action. Kant's test: imagine the maxim as a law everyone follows. Some maxims can't even be thought that way. His example is a lying promise: if everyone made false promises when in need, no one would believe a promise, and the maxim would defeat itself. Others can be thought but not consistently willed, such as never helping anyone, since you yourself will someday need help.

blocks.name: gb-maxim-test
blocks.cap: Kant's four examples and more. Run each maxim through the test: can it be a universal law? Could you will it?

blocks.html: Kant thinks this second formula comes to the same thing as the first. A third adds that each rational being is a law-maker in a kingdom of ends: the moral law is not imposed from outside but is reason's own law. That is what Kant calls autonomy, and why he says only beings who give themselves the law have dignity.

The second Critique argues that the moral law shows we are free: "ought" implies "can." Kant also says practical reason must hope that virtue and happiness will finally fit together, which leads him to "postulate" God and the immortality of the soul, not as things proved, but as hopes reason needs for moral life. Its conclusion holds his most famous sentence:

Thinking Kant's test asks whether the results would be bad if everyone did something. His first test asks whether the maxim could even work, or be willed without contradiction, as a law for all. It looks at the form of the rule, not at adding up consequences.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Kant's strictness drew questions. In a short essay (1797) he said one may not lie even to a murderer asking where a friend is hiding; most readers, including many of his admirers, think this goes too far, and some argue Kant's own principles allow a different answer. Hegel complained that the universal law test is "empty": almost any maxim can be phrased to pass. Utilitarians such as John Stuart Mill, in the next era, judged actions by their consequences for happiness, the main rival to Kant's view ever since.

Defenders reply that Kant captured something many people believe: that persons have a dignity that can't be traded away, that moral rules apply to everyone equally, and that motive matters. The idea of human dignity in many later declarations of rights owes a good deal to him.

items: Is an action good because of its motive, its results, or both?
Can it ever be right to break a promise?
What does it mean to treat someone as an end and not only as a means?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Think of a time you did the right thing even though no one would have known. Why did you?
  2. Is it all right to be nice to someone only because you want something from them?
  3. What if everyone cut in line? What would happen to lines?
  4. Kant said we should treat people as ends, not tools. What's an example of treating someone as a tool?
  5. Kant was amazed by the stars and by the moral law. What fills you with wonder?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
When you see a sunset and say "That's beautiful!", what are you saying? Are you saying something about the sunset, or about you? Immanuel Kant wrote a book about this.

Kant noticed that liking candy is different from finding a flower beautiful. If you like candy and I don't, fine: tastes differ. But when you call a flower beautiful, you speak as if everyone ought to agree, even though you can't prove it with reasons.

Kant also wrote about the sublime: things so huge or powerful, like a storm at sea, a towering mountain or the night sky, that they almost overwhelm us. From a safe place, they make us feel small and yet strangely great, because our minds can think of something even bigger: the infinite.

blocks.name: gb-beauty-sublime
blocks.cap: Choose a scene. Is it pleasant, beautiful or sublime, in Kant's sense?

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Beauty walk. Go outside and each find one thing you think is beautiful. Bring it back or describe it. Can you give a reason why others should find it beautiful too? Is that easy or hard? Then look up at the clouds or the night sky. Does anything feel "sublime"?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Kant's first Critique was about knowledge of nature; his second, about morality and freedom. The Critique of Judgment (1790) tries to bridge them through the power of judgment: fitting particular things under general ideas. It has two parts: judgments of taste (the beautiful and the sublime) and judgments of purpose in nature, especially in living things.

Kant analyzes the judgment "this is beautiful" in four "moments." It is disinterested: the pleasure doesn't depend on wanting to own or use the thing. It claims universal agreement. It finds in the object a purposiveness without purpose: it seems designed, but for no purpose we can name. And its claim is necessary, resting on a sense we all share.

head: Pleasant (agreeable)
Beautiful
Good
rows: free play of imagination and understanding
a concept of what it should be
the taste of a favorite food
a useful tool, a kind act
blocks.cap: Kant's three kinds of liking

blocks.html: Kant distinguishes the mathematically sublime, the vastly great, such as the starry sky or the pyramids seen up close, which our imagination can't take in at one glance, and the dynamically sublime, overwhelming power such as storms, volcanoes and waterfalls, which we find sublime only when we are safe. Either way, he says, the feeling points to something in us: reason's idea of the infinite and our moral freedom, which no force of nature can master.

blocks.name: gb-beauty-sublime
blocks.cap: Slide from small and gentle to vast and powerful. Where does the beautiful end and the sublime begin?

blocks.html: Fine art, Kant says, must look as free as nature, and it is the work of genius, a talent that gives the rule to art rather than following rules. In the second part he argues that living things seem to us to be organized for purposes: each part exists for the whole and the whole for the parts, as a tree makes its own leaves. We can't explain this by mechanism alone, he thought, so we must judge living things as if they were designed, while knowing that this is a guide for our inquiry, not proof of a designer.
Thinking Kant said beauty is just personal taste. He said the opposite of the pleasant: a judgment of beauty claims everyone's agreement, though it can't be proved by rules or concepts.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Critique of Judgment became a founding book of modern aesthetics. The Romantic poets and painters took up the sublime (the Art Ladder's rung on Romanticism shows paintings of storms and mountains). Schiller built a theory of education on Kant's idea of free play. In biology, Kant's remark that it is absurd to hope "another Newton will arise" who could explain a blade of grass living things by mechanical laws alone was later challenged by Darwin's theory of natural selection, which explains the appearance of design without a designer; that debate continues in the next era.

items: When two people disagree about whether something is beautiful, can one of them be wrong?
Why might we feel great in front of something that makes us feel small?
Does a living thing have purposes, or does it only seem to?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is the most beautiful thing you have seen? Could you convince someone else?
  2. Is liking pizza the same kind of thing as finding a song beautiful?
  3. Have you ever felt the sublime, in a storm, at the ocean, under the stars?
  4. Why do you think the sublime only works when we are safe?
  5. Can a drawing follow every rule and still not be beautiful?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Gulliver's Travels is satire for grown-ups as well as children. A few scenes have rough bodily humor, and the fourth voyage is bitter about human nature. The voyages to Lilliput and Brobdingnag read well aloud with young readers; preview the rest.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Lemuel Gulliver is a ship's doctor who keeps getting shipwrecked in very strange places. On his first voyage he wakes up on a beach in Lilliput, tied down by hundreds of threads. The people there are about six inches tall!

To them Gulliver is a giant, the "Man-Mountain." They feed him huge meals and argue about silly things, like which end of a boiled egg to crack: the big end or the little end. Swift was poking fun at how people in his own country quarreled over small things.

On his second voyage Gulliver reaches Brobdingnag, where everyone is as tall as a church steeple, and now he is the tiny one. A kind girl named Glumdalclitch takes care of him like a doll. The giant king listens to Gulliver brag about England and isn't impressed at all.

blocks.name: gb-gulliver-scale
blocks.cap: Choose a voyage and compare Gulliver with the people he meets.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Lilliput math. The Lilliputians are 12 times smaller than Gulliver. Measure a grown-up's height and divide by 12: that's how tall a Lilliputian would be next to them. Cut out a paper Lilliputian that size. Then try it the other way: a Brobdingnagian is 12 times taller. How tall would one be next to you? Would they fit in your house?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: A satire disguised as a travel book

blocks.html: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745) was an Anglo-Irish clergyman, Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, and the sharpest satirist of his age. Gulliver's Travels (1726) imitates the travel books that were popular then, with maps, measurements and a plain-spoken narrator. Many readers at first took it as a true story. Swift said he wrote it "to vex the world rather than divert it."
Gulliver, about twelve times taller than the Lilliputians, is a marvel and a burden to them. Swift's numbers are careful:

blocks.title: The Lilliputians' arithmetic
blocks.q: If Gulliver is 12 times as tall as a Lilliputian, and the same shape, how many Lilliputians' worth of body is he?
steps: Every length (height, width, depth) is 12 times as great.
Volume grows as length × width × depth: $12 \times 12 \times 12 = 12^3$.

blocks.html: Lilliput's politics are a small mirror of Britain's: officials win office by rope-dancing; two parties are divided by the height of their shoe heels; and a long war with the island of Blefuscu began over the right end at which to break an egg. Gulliver captures Blefuscu's fleet but refuses to help enslave its people, and he falls out of favor.

Now Gulliver is the small one. The giants' skin looks coarse to him up close, and he fights off rats and wasps. The king hears his proud account of England's government, laws and wars and is shocked. The king's own wisdom is practical:

blocks.name: gb-gulliver-scale
blocks.cap: Lilliput (1 : 12) and Brobdingnag (12 : 1). Slide between the voyages: sizes scale by 12, areas by 144, volumes by 1728.

blocks.text: Part III: Laputa and Part IV: the Houyhnhnms

blocks.html: In Part III Gulliver visits Laputa, a flying island whose rulers are so lost in mathematics and music that servants must flap them with bladders to make them listen, and the Academy of Lagado, where projectors try to extract sunbeams from cucumbers. It mocks learning cut off from common sense. In Part IV he reaches a land ruled by wise, calm horses, the Houyhnhnms, who live by reason, and finds there brutish creatures in human form, the Yahoos. Gulliver comes home disgusted with people and prefers the company of his horses.
Satire holds up human folly to laughter in order to correct it. Swift's method is the change of scale: by making people tiny, huge, or seen through a horse's eyes, he makes the familiar look strange.

Taking Gulliver's view at the end as Swift's own. Many readers think Swift is mocking Gulliver too: he becomes ridiculous in his scorn for his family. Readers still argue about how far Swift shared it.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: How the book has been read

blocks.html: Children have loved Lilliput and Brobdingnag for three centuries, usually in shortened versions. Adult readers have argued over Part IV: is it a hatred of humankind, or a warning against pride, including the pride of thinking we can live by reason alone? Swift wrote to Alexander Pope that he hated "that animal called man" but heartily loved individual people.

Scientists like the book's scale problem. Galileo had already shown (in Two New Sciences, on this ladder) that a giant twelve times taller couldn't simply be a scaled-up person: its weight grows as the cube of its size but the strength of its bones only as the square, so its legs would break. Swift's Brobdingnagians walk about happily anyway.

items: Why might it be easier to see our own faults in a made-up country?
Who is wiser, the king of Brobdingnag or Gulliver?
Is reason alone enough to make a good life, as the Houyhnhnms think?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which of Gulliver's lands would you most like to visit? Why?
  2. The Lilliputians fought a war over how to crack an egg. What are some silly things people argue about?
  3. How did Gulliver feel when he was the giant? How did he feel when he was the tiny one?
  4. Why do you think the king of Brobdingnag was not impressed by Gulliver's stories about England?
  5. Is it fair to make fun of people to help them see their mistakes?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Candide is a short, fast satire in which wars, an earthquake and many cruelties happen in quick succession, told briefly and with dark comedy, and some scenes involve mistreatment of women. We summarize those parts without detail. Preview before reading it with children; the opening chapters and the ending in the garden are good to read together.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Candide is a kind, simple young man who grows up in a castle in Germany. His teacher, Doctor Pangloss, tells him that everything that happens is for the best, in "the best of all possible worlds."

Then Candide is thrown out of the castle and goes around the whole world. He meets storms, an earthquake, wars and many unkind people. Each time Pangloss says it was all for the best. Candide starts to wonder.

He even finds a hidden land called El Dorado, where gold lies on the roads like pebbles and everyone lives in peace. At the end Candide and his friends settle on a small farm. They stop arguing about big ideas, and Candide says: "We must cultivate our garden." Working together, they are finally content.

blocks.name: gb-candide-map
blocks.cap: Follow Candide's journey around the world, from Westphalia to the little garden near Constantinople.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Plant a garden. Plant a seed in a cup of soil or tend a real garden patch. Each day, do one small job for it. Talk about Candide's last words: why might working on something small and real make people happier than arguing about whether everything is for the best?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), the most famous writer of the French Enlightenment: poet, playwright, historian and campaigner against intolerance and unjust trials. He published Candide, or Optimism in 1759, anonymously; it was banned in several places and sold widely anyway.

Its target is a philosophy of optimism, the claim, associated with the philosopher Leibniz and the poet Alexander Pope, that this is the best of all possible worlds and that every evil serves a larger good. The great Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which killed tens of thousands, had made Voltaire ask how anyone could say that to the people who suffered.

Expelled from the castle for kissing the Baron's daughter, Cunégonde, Candide is forced into an army, sees a war, survives a shipwreck and the Lisbon earthquake, and flees to South America. In El Dorado he finds a peaceful, wise people who have no priests to quarrel and no courts or prisons; he leaves with treasure to rescue Cunégonde, and loses most of it to cheats. His companions include Cacambo, his loyal servant, and Martin, a gloomy scholar who thinks the world is mostly evil. Pangloss reappears again and again, battered but still insisting all is for the best.

blocks.name: gb-candide-map
blocks.cap: Candide's route, stop by stop. Each stop has its own target of satire.

blocks.html: In the end the friends live together on a little farm near Constantinople. A wise old Turk tells them that work keeps away three great evils: boredom, vice and poverty. Pangloss still makes speeches, but Candide has the last word:

Voltaire's method. Disasters come so fast and are told so flatly that the reader laughs, then notices what is being described. Each episode mocks something: war, religious persecution, greed, snobbery, and above all a philosophy that explains suffering away.

Reading the garden as giving up on the world. Many readers take it as practical advice: stop endless arguing about whether all is for the best, and do useful work that makes things better where you are.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Leibniz's defenders point out that he never said each event is good, only that God chose the best world possible on the whole, with the fewest evils needed for the greatest good. Pangloss is a cartoon of that argument. Voltaire's reply, in effect, is that a theory that can explain every disaster as for the best explains nothing and comforts no one. Rousseau, later in this era, wrote to Voltaire defending providence after Lisbon; the problem of evil the two argued about is as old as the Book of Job and appears throughout this ladder, from Augustine to Dostoevsky.

items: Can good come out of bad things? Does that make the bad things good?
Why does Candide finally stop listening to Pangloss?
What does "cultivate our garden" mean for you?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Pangloss says everything is for the best. Do you agree? Why or why not?
  2. Why do you think Candide left El Dorado, even though it was so peaceful?
  3. Who is wiser, Pangloss or Martin? Or neither?
  4. What "garden" could you take care of in your own life?
  5. Why might someone use jokes to talk about very sad things?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Denis Diderot was a French writer who spent twenty-five years making a giant book of everything people knew, the Encyclopedia. He also wrote a funny, strange conversation that he never published.

In it, a thoughtful philosopher called Me meets a man called Him at a café in Paris, where people come to watch chess. Him is the nephew of a famous composer, Rameau. He is clever, a wonderful mimic, and very poor.

Him acts out whole operas by himself, playing every instrument and singing every part, until a crowd gathers. But he also says that being good is foolish and that he would rather flatter rich people for a free dinner. Me tries to argue with him. Who wins? Diderot lets the reader decide.

blocks.name: gb-me-him
blocks.cap: Who said it? Sort each idea to Me (the philosopher) or Him (the nephew).

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Two voices. Pick a question, such as "Is it better to be honest or popular?" One person argues one side as strongly as they can, and the other argues the opposite. Then switch sides! Talk about it: is it easier to argue for what you believe, or against it?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: A dialogue with a strange history

blocks.html: Diderot (1713–1784) edited the Encyclopédie (1751–1772), a huge work of the French Enlightenment that set out the arts, sciences and trades and was repeatedly banned. He wrote Rameau's Nephew over many years, probably between about 1761 and 1774, and kept it private. It was first published in 1805, in a German translation by Goethe; the French text appeared later, and Diderot's own manuscript turned up in a Paris bookstall in 1890.

About quotations. We could not confirm a public-domain English translation of this work that can be read online, so this rung describes it in our own words and quotes nothing. Look for English translations in a library (see the box at the top of the page).

The narrator, Me (Moi), is a philosopher who believes that virtue and happiness go together. Him (Lui), the nephew of the composer Jean-Philippe Rameau, is a real person whom Diderot knew: talented, penniless, living by entertaining wealthy patrons. In the café de la Régence, by the chess players, they talk for an afternoon about music, education, genius, money and morals.

Him is shameless and brilliant. He says that in a society where everyone flatters the powerful, a man is a fool not to do the same; he describes the "positions" people take, like dancers, to please those above them; and he mocks Me's virtue as a luxury of people who can afford it. Yet he also admits he is unhappy, envies his uncle's genius, and speaks with real grief of his late wife.

The talk often turns into performance. Him mimes a violinist, a harpsichord player, a whole opera house, until the chess players stop to watch. These scenes made the book famous. Diderot also uses them to argue a point he cared about: that the new Italian comic opera, with its natural melody, was better than the stiff French style of the elder Rameau.

blocks.name: gb-me-him
blocks.cap: Sort claims from the dialogue (in our own summaries) to the speaker who makes them.

blocks.html: A dialogue without a winner. Unlike many philosophical dialogues, this one doesn't end with the wise speaker proving his case. Me gives Him good answers, but Him's attacks are never fully refuted. The reader must weigh them.

Assuming Me speaks for Diderot and Him is simply the villain. Many readers think Diderot put parts of himself into both, including his own doubts about whether a good man can thrive in a corrupt society.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Goethe translated it; Hegel, in the next era, used Him as a picture of a mind that sees through every pretense of its society and is torn apart by it, and Marx and Freud admired it too. Readers have seen in the nephew a first portrait of a modern type: the clever outsider who mocks every value but can find none to live by. The book also raises a question the Enlightenment hoped to answer: can reason and virtue make people happy when society rewards flattery?

items: Can a person be very talented and still unhappy? Why?
Is it ever smart to be dishonest? Is it ever right?
Why might a writer let the "wrong" side argue well?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think Diderot never published this dialogue?
  2. Him says good people are foolish. How would you answer him?
  3. Is it fair to judge someone who flatters others because he is poor and hungry?
  4. What makes a conversation interesting to listen to?
  5. Can you be very good at something and still feel like a failure?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Montesquieu was a French judge and nobleman who spent twenty years on one giant question: why do different countries have different laws?

He decided that good laws must fit the people who live under them: their kind of government, their climate and land, their work, their customs and their religion. A law that works well in one place might fail in another.

He also had a famous idea about keeping people free. Power should not all be in one person's hands. Split it into three: one group makes the laws, one carries them out, and one judges. Then each part can check the others, so no one can become a bully.

blocks.name: gb-three-powers
blocks.cap: Give the three powers to different people, or put them in one hand, and see what Montesquieu says happens to freedom.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Three-part game. Play a simple game where one person makes up the rules, a second person is the referee who decides if the rules were broken, and a third is the scorekeeper. Then play again where one person does all three jobs. Which game feels fairer? Why?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu (1689–1755), was a judge in the parliament of Bordeaux. He became famous for the Persian Letters (1721), a satire of French society through the eyes of two Persian visitors, then traveled through Europe and spent nearly two years in England. The Spirit of Laws (1748), in 31 books, was translated into English by Thomas Nugent in 1750. The Catholic Church placed it on its Index of forbidden books in 1751, and it was read and argued over across Europe and America.

blocks.text: Three kinds of government, three principles

blocks.html: Montesquieu sorts governments by their nature (who holds power) and their principle (the passion that makes them work):

head: Government
Who rules
Its principle
rows: the people, or part of them
virtue: love of country and of equality
one person, by his own will
blocks.cap: Montesquieu's three types (Books II–III)

blocks.html: Laws should suit the principle: a republic needs education in public virtue, a monarchy needs ranks and the courts that defend them, and despotism needs little law at all. Later books relate laws to climate (Books XIV–XVII), soil, commerce, religion and population. Many of his claims about climate and national character are now rejected, but the idea that laws must be studied in their whole social setting was new and lasting.

blocks.text: Liberty and the separation of powers

blocks.html: Political liberty, Montesquieu says, is not doing whatever one wants, but the security of living under laws, the feeling that one need not be afraid of another citizen. Experience teaches that anyone with power tends to abuse it:
In Book XI, ch. 6, describing the constitution of England as he understood it, he names three powers: the legislative, the executive and the power of judging:

blocks.name: gb-three-powers
blocks.cap: Combine any two powers, or all three, and read Montesquieu's warning for each case.

blocks.html: He adds that judging should not be joined to either other power, or the judge would be a legislator or an oppressor. He praises England's two-house legislature, the executive's veto and trial by jury. Historians note that his picture of England was partly idealized: the English ministers already sat in Parliament.

Montesquieu thought commerce softens manners and inclines nations to peace. Book XV attacks slavery with bitter irony, listing the "arguments" of slaveholders in a way that exposes them. His constant advice is moderation: sudden, sweeping changes in law are dangerous, and the best laws suit a people as it is.

Thinking Montesquieu invented checks and balances from nothing. He drew on Locke, on ancient writers and on what he saw in England; his gift was to set the three powers out clearly as a rule for liberty.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Studies of American political writing in the 1760s–1800s find Montesquieu among the authors the founders cited most. In The Federalist No. 47, Madison calls him "the celebrated Montesquieu" and the "oracle" on separation of powers, and argues that the powers must be separate but not wholly unconnected, so that each can check the others. The Anti-Federalists also cited him, arguing that he showed a republic must be small; Madison's answer in No. 10, on the Federalist rung, is that a large republic can protect liberty better.

Some readers find the book disorderly, with many chapters only a paragraph long. Others criticize its climate theory and its use of travelers' tales about distant peoples. Defenders reply that Montesquieu was among the first to study law as a social science, comparing many societies to find the causes behind their laws.

items: Why might it be dangerous for one person to make, enforce and judge the rules?
Should laws be the same everywhere, or fit each people?
What makes people feel free under a government?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. In your family or classroom, who makes the rules, who makes sure they're followed, and who settles arguments?
  2. Why might even a good person misuse power if no one can check it?
  3. Montesquieu said laws should fit the people. Can you think of a rule that fits one place but not another?
  4. What does it mean to feel safe from other people? Why did Montesquieu call that liberty?
  5. Is it better to change laws slowly or quickly? Why?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva, a small city-republic, and became one of the most famous writers in France. He asked: Why are some people rich and others poor? Why do some rule and others obey? Was it always this way?

Rousseau imagined the very first people, living alone in the forests long ago. They needed little, were healthy and free, and felt pity when they saw others suffer. Then, little by little, people built huts, lived in families and villages, and began to compare themselves: who sings best, who is strongest, who is most admired.
Then came farming and tools of iron. One day someone put a fence around a piece of land and said, "This is mine." Rousseau said that was the start of a long road to inequality.

blocks.name: gb-inequality
blocks.cap: Step through Rousseau's story of how inequality began.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The fence game. Lay out a blanket as "the land." Put snacks on it. First, everyone shares freely. Then let one person mark off a corner with string and say "This is mine." How do the others feel? What rules would you make to keep things fair? Talk about Rousseau's question: should anyone have pulled up the stakes?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Rousseau (1712–1778) won fame with a prize essay, the Discourse on the Arts and Sciences (1750), which argued, against the spirit of his age, that the progress of the arts and sciences had not made people better. Volume 35 contains two later works: the Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755), written for a prize question from the Academy of Dijon, and the Discourse on Political Economy (1755), an article for Diderot's Encyclopédie.

Hobbes had said people in the state of nature would be at war, and Locke that they would already have property. Rousseau says both put into the state of nature ideas that only society gives. He asks us to set aside the facts of history and imagine "natural man": solitary, strong, with few needs, moved by two feelings, self-preservation and pity at the suffering of others, and marked by a capacity Rousseau calls perfectibility, the power to change and develop.

Two kinds of self-love. Rousseau distinguishes amour de soi, a natural care for oneself, from amour-propre, the self-love that compares itself with others and wants to be thought better. He sees amour-propre as the root of vanity, envy and much social inequality.

Rousseau adds at once that the idea of property depended on many earlier steps. Huts and families brought the first comparisons and the wish to be esteemed. Agriculture and metalworking divided labor and made people depend on each other. Property brought rich and poor, and conflict. Then, Rousseau says, the rich proposed a clever plan: laws and a government to keep the peace for everyone, which in fact fixed their own advantages in place. Inequality ended, in his story, in despotism.

blocks.name: gb-inequality
blocks.cap: Rousseau's stages from the solitary savage to the first government. Notice where comparison and property enter.

blocks.html: Here Rousseau first sets out the idea of the general will: the will of the body politic for the common good, which should guide laws. Good government, he says, makes citizens love their country through education and fair laws, and taxes should fall more lightly on the necessities of the poor than on the luxuries of the rich.

Saying Rousseau wanted people to go back to living in forests. He says plainly that this is impossible for us. His aim was to show that much inequality is made by society, not by nature, and so might be judged and changed.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Voltaire, sent a copy, wrote back that no one had ever used so much wit to make us want to walk on all fours. Many later thinkers took up Rousseau's question about the causes of inequality, including Adam Smith, the next rung, who reviewed the Discourse, and Marx in the next era. Critics say his state of nature is a myth with no evidence; Rousseau called it a hypothesis to help us judge the present, not a history.
Modern study of early human societies paints a more varied picture than any one 18th-century story, and scholars still debate how inequality arose with farming and settled life.

items: Is inequality natural, made by people, or both?
Does comparing ourselves with others make us better or unhappier?
Did the first fence-builder do something wrong?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Rousseau said comparing ourselves to others can make us unhappy. Do you agree?
  2. What do you think the world was like before anyone owned land?
  3. Is it fair that some people have more than others? When is it fair, and when not?
  4. Rousseau thought pity is natural. Do you think people are naturally kind?
  5. If you could make one rule to keep things fair among friends, what would it be?

Rousseau's most famous book begins with a startling sentence: "Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains." He meant that people are born with freedom, but live under rulers and laws they didn't choose.

Rousseau asked: how could people live together under laws and still be free? His answer was a kind of promise, a social contract. Everyone joins together and agrees to obey laws that the whole people makes for the good of all. When you obey a law that you helped make, you are obeying yourself.
Rousseau called the people's shared wish for the common good the general will. It isn't just what most people want at the moment. It is what is good for everyone together.

blocks.name: gb-sovereign-share
blocks.cap: Change the number of citizens and see each person's share of the vote.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A class law. As a family, decide on one rule that everyone will keep for a week (for example, "Phones stay out of the kitchen at dinner"). Everyone gets a vote, and the rule applies to everyone, grown-ups too. At the end of the week, talk: did it feel different to follow a rule you helped make?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

The Social Contract (1762) appeared the same year as Rousseau's novel on education, Emile. Both were condemned and burned in Paris and in his native Geneva, and Rousseau fled. The book's question is not how governments began, but what could make them legitimate:

Force can't make right, Rousseau argues: if might made right, the right would vanish the moment the might did. Nor can a people give itself away to a master, since giving up one's freedom is giving up being human.

blocks.text: The contract and the general will

blocks.html: The solution is a contract in which each person gives himself and all his rights to the whole community, so that the conditions are the same for all and no one has an interest in making them burdensome. In return each becomes an equal member of the sovereign, the people as law-maker. Rousseau distinguishes the general will, which aims at the common interest, from the will of all, which is only the sum of private wishes. The general will can't be represented: laws must be approved by the people themselves.

Key terms. Sovereign: the whole people making law. Government: the officials who carry out the law, a go-between, never the sovereign itself. General will: the will for the common good. Law: an act of the general will about matters common to all.

Rousseau's most troubling line says that whoever refuses to obey the general will "shall be compelled to do so by the whole body," which, he says, "means nothing less than that he will be forced to be free" (Book I, ch. 7). Readers have argued over it ever since.
In Book III Rousseau turns to government. He uses a bit of arithmetic to show why large states are harder to keep free:

blocks.name: gb-sovereign-share
blocks.cap: Rousseau's ratio: each citizen's share of sovereignty is 1 / N. The larger the state, the smaller the share, though each is still wholly under the law.

blocks.html: Democracy, aristocracy and monarchy each suit different sizes of state; Rousseau thinks true democracy fits only a small people of great virtue, and that elective aristocracy is often the best government. The book ends with a chapter on civil religion: a short public creed (a God, a life to come, the sanctity of the social contract and the laws) together with tolerance of all religions that tolerate others. Critics have found this chapter one of the hardest to square with freedom of conscience.
Confusing the general will with majority vote. A vote is Rousseau's way of finding the general will, and he says it works only when citizens vote for the common good and are not split into factions.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Leaders of the French Revolution, especially the Jacobins, honored Rousseau and moved his remains to the Panthéon in 1794. Kant admired him so much that, it was said, he once skipped his daily walk to keep reading Emile. Supporters see in the Social Contract a powerful case for popular sovereignty, equality before the law and citizenship as active self-government.

Critics, among them Benjamin Constant in the 19th century and several 20th-century historians, argued that the general will and "forced to be free" could be used to justify states that override individual rights in the name of the people. Defenders answer that Rousseau insists on laws applying equally to all and on the sovereign's limits. Comparing Rousseau with Locke and Montesquieu, who stress representation and divided powers, is one of the great debates of this era.

items: Can you be free while obeying laws?
What's the difference between what everyone wants and what's good for everyone?
Why might large groups make it harder for each person to have a say?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What does "born free, and everywhere in chains" mean to you?
  2. Have you ever followed a rule you helped make? Did it feel different?
  3. Is what most people want always what is best for everyone?
  4. Rousseau said each citizen's share of power shrinks as a country grows. Is that a problem? How could it be helped?
  5. What do you think of the idea of being "forced to be free"?

Adam Smith was a Scottish professor who wanted to know: what makes a country rich? Not gold piled up in a king's treasury, he said, but all the useful things its people make and trade.

He started with something tiny: a pin. One worker alone, making pins from start to finish, could hardly make one pin a day, and certainly not twenty. But in a pin factory Smith visited, ten workers each did one or two steps, cutting wire, sharpening points, putting on heads, and together they made about 48,000 pins a day!

Smith called this the division of labor. When people specialize and then trade, everyone can have more. The baker bakes, the butcher cuts meat, and they trade, each helping the other while helping themselves.

blocks.name: gb-pin-factory
blocks.cap: Split the eighteen steps of pin-making among more workers and watch the day's output.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Paper-airplane factory. Time one person making five paper airplanes from start to finish. Then split the job: one person folds the first creases, one does the wings, one decorates. Time five planes again. Which way was faster? Was any job boring? (Smith worried about that too.)

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Adam Smith (1723–1790) taught moral philosophy at Glasgow and first became known for The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), a book about sympathy and conscience. An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations appeared in 1776, the year of the American Declaration of Independence. It argues against mercantilism, the policy of piling up gold and silver through trade surpluses, protecting home industries and granting monopolies.

blocks.title: Smith's pin numbers
blocks.q: Ten workers make about twelve pounds of pins a day, with upwards of 4,000 pins in a pound. How many pins is that per worker?
steps: $12 \times 4000 = 48{,}000$ pins a day for the ten.
Working alone, Smith says, each could certainly not make twenty: $4800 \div 20 = 240$, so at least 240 times as many.
blocks.a: 4,800 pins each, about 240 times what one could make alone

blocks.html: Smith gives three reasons the division of labor raises output: greater skill from doing one task, time saved in not switching tasks, and the invention of machines by workers focused on one job. And it is limited by the extent of the market: a village can't support a full-time pin-maker, a great trading city can.

People have, Smith says, a natural "propensity to truck, barter, and exchange." Prices tend toward a natural price that covers wages, profit and rent, though the market price rises and falls with supply and demand. In Book IV he says that a merchant who seeks only his own gain is often "led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention": the good of society. The phrase appears only once in the book.

blocks.name: gb-pin-factory
blocks.cap: How output depends on dividing the work. Smith's real figures: fewer than 20 pins a day alone, about 4,800 each in the factory.

blocks.text: The system of natural liberty, and its limits

blocks.html: Smith favors a "system of natural liberty" in which each person may pursue his own interest within the laws of justice. But he assigns the government real duties: defense, the administration of justice, and public works and institutions that private profit wouldn't provide, including roads, harbors and schooling for the common people. He warns that merchants and manufacturers often conspire to raise prices and seek monopolies from government, and that the repetitive work of the division of labor can dull workers' minds unless education counters it.

Thinking Smith said greed is good or that government should do nothing. He wrote a whole book on sympathy and virtue, and he gave government important tasks; he thought free exchange within just laws served the public better than monopolies and trade restrictions.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

The Wealth of Nations is often called the founding book of modern economics. British trade policy moved toward freer trade in the 19th century, partly under its influence. Later economists kept Smith's questions but changed many answers: his theory of value, which gave labor a central place, was developed by Ricardo and then by Marx (in the next era) in a direction Smith did not take, while later economists explained prices by supply and demand at the margin.

Economists today still argue about how far markets should be left free and where government should step in, for public goods, monopolies, or helping those left behind. Both sides often claim Smith, and his own mixed view is a reason to read him directly.

items: Why does trading make both sides better off?
Is specializing always good for the worker?
What should government do that markets won't?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What jobs in your home are "divided"? Does dividing them help?
  2. When you buy bread, why does the baker sell it to you?
  3. Smith worried that doing one small task all day is dull. How could that be helped?
  4. What makes a country rich, in Smith's view? Do you agree?
  5. Can doing something for yourself also help others? Give an example.

In 1776 thirteen American colonies decided to break away from Great Britain. Thomas Jefferson wrote a statement explaining why, and the Continental Congress approved it on July 4, 1776. It is the Declaration of Independence.
It says that all people are created equal, with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments get their power from the people they govern.

The new states first joined under the Articles of Confederation, a loose friendship of states with a weak national government. It didn't work well, so in 1787 leaders met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution, which still guides the United States today, with three branches of government and, soon after, the Bill of Rights.

blocks.name: gb-founding
blocks.cap: Step through the founding years, from the Declaration to the Bill of Rights.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Write a family charter. Together, write a short "preamble" for your family that begins "We the people of the ____ household, in order to…" and lists what you want your family to be. Sign it and hang it up. Then read the real Preamble together and compare.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Volume 40 opens with three founding documents of the United States. They are not one book by one author but the work of many people over fifteen years, and they show a new nation arguing its way to a form of government. The American History & Civics Ladder covers them in detail; here we read them as great books.

head: Document
Date
What it did
rows: explained why the colonies separated from Britain
joined the states in a "firm league of friendship"
created a stronger federal government of three branches
the first ten amendments, protecting rights

blocks.html: The Declaration's argument has a clear shape: a statement of principles, a long list of grievances against King George III meant to show "a long train of abuses," and the conclusion that the colonies "are, and of Right ought to be Free and Independent States." Its language echoes Locke, on this era's first rung, and other writers the colonists read. Jefferson's draft was edited by a committee including John Adams and Benjamin Franklin and then by Congress, which cut, among other things, a passage blaming the king for the slave trade.

The Articles kept each state's "sovereignty, freedom, and independence." Congress had one house, with one vote per state; it could make war and treaties but could not tax, regulate trade between the states or enforce its laws. Amendments needed every state's agreement. By the mid-1780s debts, trade quarrels and unrest such as Shays' Rebellion (1786–87) convinced many that the system had to change.

Seven articles follow: Congress (I), the President (II), the courts (III), the states (IV), amendment (V), the Constitution as the supreme law (VI) and ratification (VII). The Convention reached compromises, such as equal votes for states in the Senate and votes by population in the House, and, on slavery, the three-fifths clause and a ban on ending the slave trade before 1808, which historians see as among its gravest flaws. The Bill of Rights followed in 1791, after Anti-Federalists and others pressed for written protections.

blocks.name: gb-founding
blocks.cap: From the Declaration to the Bill of Rights, step by step, with the Articles and the Convention between.

blocks.html: A change of plan. The Articles made a league of states; the Constitution, beginning "We the People," made a government that acts directly on citizens, with powers divided among three branches and between the nation and the states.
Thinking the Declaration set up the government. It announced independence and stated principles; the Articles and then the Constitution created the actual frame of government.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Many signers held people in slavery, and the Constitution protected slavery in several clauses, while the Declaration said all men are created equal. Americans have argued about that contradiction from the start. Frederick Douglass, Abraham Lincoln and the women at Seneca Falls (1848) all appealed to the Declaration's words to call the nation to live up to them, and later amendments, beginning with the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth after the Civil War, widened who was included.

items: What does "all men are created equal" mean? What did it mean in 1776?
Why did the Articles of Confederation fail?
Why might a written constitution be harder to change than ordinary laws, and is that good?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think the Declaration lists so many complaints against the king?
  2. Which of the Preamble's goals do you think is most important?
  3. What problems came from having a very weak national government?
  4. Why do you think people wanted a Bill of Rights added?
  5. How have Americans used the Declaration's words to argue for more freedom?
